How to Choose an SEO Company for Doctors in Houston

By WevTEC Review TeamPublished Dec 30, 2024Updated Oct 25, 20269 min read
On This Page
  1. The short answer
  2. How Houston patients choose a doctor
  3. What medical SEO should include
  4. What makes Houston different
  5. Questions to ask an SEO company
  6. Red flags to avoid
  7. Cost and timeline
  8. Privacy and tracking
  9. Questions people ask AI
  10. How WevTEC Fix Website Issues helps

Want a second opinion on your site? Book a free consultation

If you run a medical practice in Houston, you’ve probably had the same week a dozen times: three agencies email you, each promises “page one,” and none of them can explain what they’ll actually change on your website. This guide covers what a medical SEO engagement should include, what’s specific to Houston, the questions that separate competent agencies from resellers, and what a realistic timeline looks like.

The short answer

A good SEO company for a Houston practice starts with an audit of your Google Business Profile, website and reviews, then gives you a written plan that names specific fixes. It should cover local SEO (the map results), technical health, service and location pages written for patients, a review process, schema markup and call tracking. Ask for medical examples you can verify, short terms, full ownership of your accounts, and reports built on calls and appointment requests rather than rankings alone.

Avoid anyone who guarantees the #1 spot, wants a long contract before an audit, or plans to publish dozens of near-identical city pages.

How Houston patients actually choose a doctor

Most patients don’t pick the first name they see. They search, open a few profiles, read reviews and check the website before they call. A Tebra survey reported by Medical Economics found that 77% of patients search online before booking, and Zocdoc says patients on its platform compare an average of 21 provider profiles first.

Reviews carry much of that decision. In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 97% of consumers said they read reviews for local businesses, 41% always read them (up from 29% a year earlier), and 31% will only use a business rated 4.5 stars or higher.

Search is changing too. Pew Research found users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits where Google showed an AI summary, versus 15% when it didn’t. Fewer people scroll, so your map listing, your reviews and how clearly your site answers patient questions matter more than they did a few years ago.

What medical SEO for doctors should include

Agencies price very different work under the same word. Here’s what a complete engagement for a doctor’s office usually covers, and what you should be able to see in writing.

Google Business Profile and map results

For most practices, the map pack drives more calls than the website. The work is concrete: correct primary and secondary categories, accurate regular and holiday hours, each provider and location set up properly, services listed, real office photos and a steady flow of new reviews. Your name, address and phone number also need to match across Google, Apple Maps, Bing, Healthgrades, Vitals, WebMD and insurance directories. Mismatched suite numbers and old phone numbers are among the most common listing problems for medical offices.

Technical health of the website

Before content, the site has to work: fast pages on a phone, nothing important blocked from Google, no broken links or redirect chains, a valid SSL certificate, an appointment form that actually delivers email, and no leftover spam pages from an old hack. Older medical sites often have several of these problems at once. Our guide to fixing broken pages and links on healthcare sites covers the common ones.

Service, condition and location pages

Each major service deserves a page a patient can use: what the visit involves, who it’s for, which insurance you take and how to book. Each office location needs real local details — address, parking, hours, the providers who work there — not the same text with a different city name.

Reviews and reputation

A good agency helps you ask every satisfied patient for a review and respond without disclosing anything about them. “Glad your knee is better” confirms someone was a patient. More in how reviews improve clinic SEO.

Schema markup and AI search visibility

Structured data tells search engines what a page describes: a medical business, a physician, a location, opening hours. It doesn’t guarantee rankings or a mention in ChatGPT, but it makes your details easier to read correctly. The bigger factor for AI answers is plain, specific content stated on the page. See how schema markup helps doctors rank locally and E-E-A-T for medical websites.

Tracking that measures patients, not traffic

Rankings and visits are easy to inflate. What matters is how many calls, form submissions and booking requests came from search, and from which pages, measured without sending patient information to ad platforms (more on that below).

What makes SEO in Houston different

Houston isn’t one market. It’s a metro area of more than seven million people spread over a huge footprint, and patients rarely cross it for routine care. Map results follow the searcher’s location, so a practice often ranks well within a few miles of its office and drops off quickly beyond that.

  • Suburb relevance matters. Patients search for “pediatrician in Cypress” or “cardiologist Sugar Land,” not just “Houston.”
  • Competition clusters around medical hubs. The Texas Medical Center is described as the largest medical complex in the world, and big hospital systems dominate many specialty searches near it. Independent practices usually win by owning their own neighborhood.
  • Spanish-language searches are common. If your staff serves Spanish-speaking patients, a few well-written Spanish pages can reach people your competitors miss.
  • Insurance questions come early. A clear, current insurance page answers the question before a patient calls someone else.

What doesn’t work is thirty pages that say “best doctor in [suburb]” with nothing else changed. Google treats those as doorway pages.

Questions to ask before you hire an SEO company

You don’t need to understand every technical detail. You need clear answers, ideally in writing:

  1. What did your audit find on my site and profile? A serious company looks before it quotes.
  2. What will you do in the first 90 days? Expect deliverables, not “ongoing optimization.”
  3. Which medical practices have you worked with? Look them up and check their map listings.
  4. Who owns the accounts? Your profile, Analytics, Search Console, hosting and domain should be in your name.
  5. Who writes and reviews medical content? Someone at your practice should approve it.
  6. What are the contract terms, and will you sign a business associate agreement if you touch patient data?

Red flags to watch for

  • Ranking guarantees. Google’s own guidance on hiring an SEO warns that no one can guarantee a #1 ranking.
  • Long contracts before any audit. That puts all the risk on you.
  • Fake or incentivized reviews. They violate Google’s policies and the FTC’s rule on fake reviews, and can get a profile suspended.
  • Mass-produced city pages or unreviewed AI-written medical content.
  • Agency-owned accounts and reports full of impressions with no calls or bookings.

What medical SEO costs and how long it takes

Pricing depends on the number of locations, providers and specialties, local competition and how much the website needs fixing first. Compare what each proposal includes rather than the monthly fee alone.

PhaseTypical workWhat you should see
Weeks 1–4Audit, profile cleanup, technical fixes, trackingA written findings list and completed fixes
Months 2–3Service and location pages, review process, directoriesNew pages live; reviews starting to rise
Months 3–6Content, schema, internal links, profile updatesBetter map visibility near your office; more calls

These are general estimates, not promises. A site that needs a rebuild or malware cleanup will take longer.

A note on privacy and tracking

In 2022 the HHS Office for Civil Rights issued guidance on online tracking technologies on healthcare websites. A federal court vacated part of it in 2024, but HIPAA still applies wherever protected health information is involved. Keep ad pixels off appointment and portal pages, don’t send form contents to ad platforms, and check any tool that touches patient data with your compliance advisor. This isn’t legal advice.

Asked on ChatGPT, Gemini and Google

Questions practice owners ask AI about medical SEO

“Is SEO worth it for a small medical practice in Houston?”

Usually, if you have capacity for new patients. Local search is where most new patients find a practice, and the work compounds: a well-built profile and service pages keep bringing calls after the initial setup. It’s less useful if you’re fully booked or rely mostly on referrals.

“How long until my practice shows up in Google Maps?”

Profile and website fixes can move map results within a few weeks. New pages typically take three to six months to bring steady traffic, longer in competitive specialties.

“Can an SEO company guarantee my practice ranks first?”

No. Google decides rankings, and results change with each searcher’s location. A guarantee usually means a term nobody searches.

“How do I get ChatGPT to recommend my clinic?”

No one can guarantee a mention. AI tools lean on sources that state facts clearly and consistently: services, providers, locations, insurance, hours and a strong review profile, matched across your site and directories.

“Do I need a page for every Houston suburb?”

Only where you have an office or genuinely specific information. One strong page per real location beats dozens of near-duplicates.

“Should my practice use SEO or Google Ads?”

They do different jobs. Google Ads puts you on the page the day a campaign starts, but the calls stop when the budget does. SEO takes months to build and keeps working after that. Many practices run ads for high-value services while the map listing and service pages gain ground, then reduce ad spend where organic results hold.

“How do I know if my current SEO company is working?”

Look at calls and appointment requests from Google over six months, your map position for your main service near your office, and whether review volume is growing. If the monthly report shows only impressions and keyword counts, ask for those three numbers.

“What should I prepare before talking to an SEO agency?”

Owner access to your Google Business Profile, hosting, domain and Analytics, plus your most valuable services, accepted insurance plans and the areas your patients come from.
